extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology, literary studies, and creative writing instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and characterization of narrative time (order, rhythm, frequency, heterochrony) and the ways characters are presented, determined, and perceived by readers; aimed at tools for literary analysis and creative-writing practice. Emphasizes distinctions between fabula and story, forms of repetition/iteration, and how textual and extra-textual information shapes character-effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: The story overrules the fabula (presentation vs event)
rubrics_metrics.description: The story's presentation can dominate or displace the fabula (the sequence of events), so that descriptive account and nuances of perception replace the simple act in the fabula: "The story overrules the fabula here."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and examples (Proust, Woolf): slow-downs that focus on perception (e.g., a kiss) mean more time is spent describing nuances than the event itself; this can produce a "miniature new fabula" and long descriptive flows that obscure the bare chronology of events. Consider whether presentation is a pause in fabula-time or wholly covers it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm (narrative rhythm & correlation between story-time and fabula-time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative rhythm concerns temporal pacing and the correspondence (or disruption) between story-time and fabula-time; variations create different aesthetic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how slow-downs, pauses, fragmentation, or frantic pacing affect perception of events. Postmodern works (e.g., Kathy Acker) may deliberately disrupt temporal equivalence to create fragmentation, incoherence, or a postmodern 'feel.' Use examples: Proust's extended close-up vs Acker's hasty/fragmented pace. Note that simple quantitative measures of rhythm may not capture subtle literary technique (Flaubert).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency (Genette's numerical relationship between fabula and story)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequency is the numerical relationship between events as they occur in the fabula and how often they are presented in the story (i.e., repetition, singularity, iteration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Genette's distinctions and formulae (– 1f/1s: singular; – nf/ns: plurisingular; – nf/ms: varisingular; – 1f/ns: repetitive; – nf/1s: iterative). Consider paradoxes of repetition (no two events/texts are strictly identical), cinematic conventions (three occurrences imply endless repetition), and whether repetition is stylistically varied or perspectival (focalization) to justify multiple presentations. Examples: Borges quoting Don Quixote; Faulkner; Robbe-Grillet; Chopin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition vs Iteration (types and effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish repetition (one event presented multiple times) from iteration (many identical events presented in one compressed presentation); iteration can be generalizing, external, or pseudo-iterative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether iterative passages generalize about situations (e.g., Dickens' poorhouse), extend beyond fabula time-span (external iteration), or are pseudo-iterations (very long descriptive passages presented as if a frequent series occurred, e.g., Proust). Consider how iteration highlights background or makes routine dominant; iterative choices affect realism and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of iteration (generalizing, external, pseudo-iteration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three forms of iteration: (1) generalizing situation-descriptions that present facts beyond the fabula; (2) external iterations that highlight events related to fabula but beyond its time span; (3) pseudo-iteration where iterative stance is implausible because of excessive detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify iterative passages in a text into these forms. Use Dickens' Oliver Twist for generalizing, single-character histories that lie outside fabula for external iteration, and Proust's long visits as pseudo-iteration. Note rhetorical/political effects (e.g., anti-realism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterochrony (multi-temporality vs experience of multiple times)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heterochrony denotes the subjective experience of multiple, heterogeneous temporalities (as distinct from the objective phenomenon of multi-temporality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider migration, video, and modern culture as intensifiers of heterochrony; weigh both negative (inhibition, paralysis) and positive (intense, meaningful days) experiences. Argument: studying narrative temporality can develop political and cultural sensitivity to temporal disjunctions in lived experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-effect (characters as fabricated figures producing affect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are fabricated, anthropomorphic figures that produce a character-effect in readers (we 'see' characters, empathize, like/dislike), but they are not real people and should not be conflated with actual humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or creating characters, restrict investigation to what is presented in the text's words to avoid projecting extra-textual psychological traits. Allow characters to 'resist' readers rather than forcing them into familiar psychological categories. Beware of reducing characters to realism-driven psychological portraits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information sources for character construction (what forms a character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are constructed from various kinds of textual information: portraits, actions, thoughts, feelings, memories, appearance, names, work, and other data presented by the narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how each type of information contributes to the character-effect. Emphasize that 'what a figure does is as important as what he or she thinks, feels, remembers, or looks like.' Consider coherence arising from cumulative details but avoid overattributing psychological unity beyond the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why characters resist us (anthropomorphism warning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers’ tendency to treat characters as real people leads to projection, fallacies, inappropriate psychological or ideological readings, and flattening of texts (e.g., misreading ancient or non-Western narratives through modern realist expectations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytically distance from anthropomorphism; formulate ideological assumptions explicitly and use them cautiously in criticism. Recognize that resistance to full analysis is evidence of narratology's success, not failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame of reference (extra-textual communal knowledge determining character)
rubrics_metrics.description: The frame of reference is the slice of extra-textual reality or communal knowledge readers bring (historical facts, stereotypes, cultural expectations) that shapes character determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how shared knowledge (e.g., public figures, legends, historical expectations) supplies immediate character cues and influences humor, surprise, or recognition. Be attentive that different readers (age, culture) have different frames of reference, producing varying responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referential characters (historical, legendary, mythical) and their constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Referential characters occupy recognizable slots in the reader's frame of reference and are thus more strongly determined by prior expectations (e.g., Santa Claus, Napoleon); deviation from expected traits can produce surprise or destroy recognizability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use referential characters strategically: conforming to expectations yields recognizability; subverting expectations can create humor, suspense, or critique, but risks making the figure 'no longer [that character]'. Evaluate how much confrontation between prior image and textual realization the narrative intends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability and determination of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters become more or less predictable based on textual cues and extra-textual information; each piece of information limits possibilities (determination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze pronouns, names, gender, social status, occupation, exterior description, and genre conventions to see how they fix expectations. Consider how predictability shifts narrative tension from 'what will happen' to 'will the character realize or break away from its determination?' Examples: Miss Marple (name+title implying stereotypical traits), genre expectations in detective fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre's role in shaping character expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Genre conventions impose characteristic expectations about characters and their likely actions (e.g., a detective must find the murderer), which shape reader anticipation and narrative tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or crafting narratives, account for genre-bound expectations and how their fulfilment, alteration, or frustration contributes to meaning and aesthetic effect. Note examples where genre expectations are subverted (e.g., The Locked Room).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological coloring and extra-textual influence on character interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics' and readers' ideologies, knowledge, and contextual assumptions strongly color character descriptions and value judgments, often unconsciously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly recognize ideological hang-ups when making claims about characters (e.g., declaring a character 'immoral'); avoid conflating author and character; situate moral or ideological claims within textual context and broader cultural frameworks.
